content.p: In the ninth month of Lebanon's civil war, a Christian town on the coast road south of Beirut was overrun, and the people who had not fled were killed. Damour, a Maronite community of silk factories and mulberry groves, fell in January 1976 to Palestinian and leftist forces fighting their way up the coast from Sidon. Mapping MENA dates the attack to 20 January and puts the dead at between 300 and 600, mostly civilians. A Guardian reconstruction of Israeli documents describes the dead more cautiously, as 200 civilians.

The figures are not settled, and the town's story does not end with the killing. Damour was emptied of its Christians, resettled by the Palestinian side, retaken in 1982 and taken again, in a different way, by the Druze. When the reporter Robert Fisk walked through it in 1993, he found one Christian family back.
content.h2: A town on the road to Beirut
content.p: Fisk described Damour as a pretty coastal hamlet dating back to the Crusades, living from mulberry groves and silk factories along the Mediterranean. Its misfortune was geography. It stood on the highway to Beirut and blocked the path of the Palestinian and leftist forces advancing from Sidon, and Fisk called it the first town to be ethnically cleansed in the civil war.

The war itself was less than a year old. The BBC's timeline dates its start to 1975, when Phalangist gunmen ambushed a bus in Beirut's Ayn al-Rummanah district and killed 27 mainly Palestinian passengers, claiming guerrillas had earlier attacked a nearby church. As the war went on, militias split the country along religious lines. A conflict-resolution study of Mount Lebanon by Aïda Kanafani-Zahar says that between 600,000 and 800,000 people were displaced during the war, and that militias deliberately forced people out to divide the country into confessional zones. She lists Damour among the massacres that helped that process, alongside Karantina and Tel el-Zaatar.

Mapping MENA presents the attack as a response to the Karantina massacre of 18 January 1976, in which, it says, Maronite Christians attacked the PLO and Muslim groups. Fisk makes the same link and uses the Phalangists' own word for what happened at Karantina, "purification", the removal of Palestinians and Muslim Lebanese from east Beirut. In his account Damour was destroyed in revenge for that killing of Palestinians, and the sequence did not stop there: the annihilation of the Tel el-Zaatar camp, where he says Christians killed more than 2,000 prisoners, was partly in retaliation for Damour.

The sources describe the attackers differently. Mapping MENA says Muslim and left-wing militants with help from PLO units. The Guardian's note on the Israeli documents says "fighters including Palestinians". None of the pages opened names a commander or a unit.

The fullest first-hand account in the sources comes from Georges Naufal, who gave it to Fisk in 1993, standing by the broken villa where he had lived with his parents. He remembered the last night as 22 January, which differs from the date Mapping MENA gives. He told Fisk that those living in the centre of town hid in the church while shells fell, that about 450 people spent the night there with Father Labaki, and that they knew Palestinian and Muslim forces were coming and had no time to take belongings.

That day, Naufal said, his nephew Antoine Chahoub, only 20, had been killed in the old palace on the hill above the town when a rocket-propelled grenade hit him in the chest. At daybreak the people in the church ran down to the old silk factory and sheltered from the shelling there until boats sent down the coast from Jounieh and a second port took them away.

Mapping MENA quotes a priest, Father Mansour Labaky, described as a survivor, who called it "an apocalypse". He recalled attackers "coming, thousands and thousands", shouting "Allahu Akbar" and slaughtering men, women and children in their path. Mapping MENA adds that about 15,000 people fled to the sea in small boats, a number Fisk also gives for the Christians who left. The priest's name is spelled Labaki in one source and Labaky in the other; the two accounts appear to concern the same priest, though neither page says so outright.

Fisk's reconstruction is the most detailed and also the harshest. He wrote that gunmen stormed in as the Christians fled, "executing" the surviving Christian fighters and taking prisoner almost 250 civilians. He wrote that the militiamen, many of them high on hashish, separated several young women from the prisoners and gang-raped them, then slaughtered the women together with the rest of the captives. In the text saved, Fisk does not name a source for these details, and no other page opened confirms or disputes them.

Mapping MENA's version is shorter. It says twenty Phalangist men, members of a Christian militia, were executed, and that civilians were then lined up against a wall and sprayed with machine-gun fire. Its total of 300 to 600 dead covers the whole episode. That is higher than the 200 civilians in the Guardian's bracketed note, and higher than the almost 250 captives Fisk counts, although Fisk does not give an overall total for Damour.
Afterwards, Fisk wrote, the gunmen systematically blew up or burned every house in the town and, as an afterthought, dug up the local graveyard and threw its dead onto the road.

Mapping MENA says the PLO resettled Palestinian refugees in the town after the massacre. Fisk gives the sequel in more detail: the PLO resettled the survivors in Damour, and they were forced out in 1982 when the Israeli army captured it and brought back its Christian allies. For three years it was Christian again, "in ruins but infested with a rag-tag of Christian militiamen", until those militiamen were driven out by the Druze, who settled their own people among the wreckage.

By 1993, Fisk reported, most of the town was a field of crushed masonry, toppled apartments and scorched interiors, with bushes growing round empty door lintels and trees sprouting from shattered villas. Druze families were living in cracked rooms with hardboard windows. The Ministry for Displaced People had its offices at one end of the devastated main street. The minister at the time, Walid Jumblatt, whose Druze militia Fisk says played a leading role in the "cleansing" in the 1983 mountain war, Fisk reported that the ministry's computers already held 60,000 names of people wanting to go home, with 6,000 added in the previous two weeks. Some applicants wanted money to repair houses in Damour.

Naufal, then 45, was one of them. He told Fisk his was the only Christian Maronite family back in the town, under Jumblatt's protection and guarantee, and he was repairing his home and working his orchards. "The first month back, I was frightened at night," he said. "But it was my land, so I came back." Mapping MENA says residents who fled returned gradually over the years and that Damour is again predominantly Christian.
content.h2: The dead remembered in later wars
content.p: Damour kept appearing in the arguments over later massacres. Elie Hobeika, a Lebanese Forces leader, was, in The Guardian's words, "said to have been" deeply influenced by the killing of much of his family and his fiancee by Palestinian militiamen at Damour in 1976. Six years later, after the assassination of Bachir Gemayel, Phalangist militiamen entered the Sabra and Chatila camps and killed more than 1,000 people, according to the same obituary, and an Israeli state inquiry in 1983 named Hobeika as the man who personally directed it. Hobeika said before his death in a bomb attack in January 2002 that his innocence was "a core issue" and that he wanted any Belgian war crimes proceeding to go ahead.

The Guardian's 2001 documents show how Damour was also used as a defence. At a meeting on 19 September 1982, the day after the militia left the camps, Major General Amir Drori told Lebanese Forces figures and Israeli colleagues at a meeting that they should mention "what happened at Damour" when explaining the camp killings. A bracketed note in the Guardian text explains that, in 1976, fighters who included Palestinians had killed 200 civilians in that Christian village.

Fisk saw the same cycle in 1993 and drew a comparison with the war in Bosnia. Naufal agreed. "I see Bosnia-Herzegovina on the television news every night," he said, "and it's like I am reliving my own life."

No page opened describes a trial, an inquiry specific to Damour, or a named person convicted for what happened there. The identity of the units, the number of dead and even the date of the final night differ between the accounts. What the sources do agree on is the outline: a Christian town on a strategic road, taken days after Karantina, a mass flight by sea, killings of those who stayed, and a long displacement that was still being undone, family by family, in the early 1990s.
